lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- What Did They Actually Mean?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Keitma Netto Cascarelli Gomes | Lesson 17 -- What Did They Actually Mean?

listenings.text: I have been an external auditor for fifteen years, and most of my problems do not come from the numbers. They come from my questions, after somebody else repeats them. Last month I asked a client whether the bank reconciliations had been reviewed before the close. That was all. The next day, the controller told me that his team was preparing all the reconciliations again, for the whole year. Somebody had relayed my question as an instruction. So now I do two things. First, when I ask a question, I say clearly that it is only a question. Second, I ask the client to repeat it back in their own words. If they say, you want to know if the review happened, we are fine. If they say, you want us to do the reconciliations again, we have a misunderstanding, and we fix it in thirty seconds instead of three days.

I coordinate a BPO team in Krakow that posts journal entries for six countries, and every day I receive instructions from controllers I have never met. The difficult ones are not the long ones. They are the short ones. Last week, a controller wrote: please fix the accruals. Which accruals? Fix them how? By when? So I wrote back. I asked him which entity he meant, and whether he wanted us to reverse the entries or only to adjust them. He was not happy at first, but he answered in ten minutes. Here is my advice. When you pass on an instruction, say who asked, what exactly they asked for, and by when. And if you are not sure what somebody meant, do not guess. Asking for clarification costs one email. Guessing can cost you the close.
